author: Ross Gay
en_title: The Book of Delights: The Writer Laughs at Himself
zh_deck: 一场赢得不太光彩的篮球赛，一株上了飞机的番茄苗。Ross Gay把小事写得迂回又好笑，也让自己的判断不断被眼前的经验修正。
en_deck: An unimpressive basketball triumph and a tomato plant on a plane: Ross Gay follows small events into memory, amusement, and corrections to his own first thoughts.

zh_title: 《欢喜之书》：写着写着，他先笑了
zh_body:
Ross Gay和朋友打篮球，把对手打了个二十一比零。他写这场大胜，兴致很高，接着才交代：对面是两个十二岁的孩子。旁边看球的女孩对他们的战绩毫不买账。

这一点点难堪，颇能说明《欢喜之书》的脾气。Gay没有把欢喜写成特别高尚的体验，也不急着从打球中总结人生。他先让自己得意一会儿，再让读者看见这份得意有多可笑。文章中的他，常常热情过头、联想太多，话说出去以后又追上去改。他喜欢的事有时候实在不值一提，可他有本领让人想听听，究竟怎么不值一提。

这和书名容易引起的预期不太一样。一本叫《欢喜之书》的书，似乎应该告诉我们怎样从日常小事里获得幸福。Gay确实写花草、食物、陌生人的好意，不过，他首先是一位诗人。这本书的趣味，相当一部分就在于他怎样把一件小事写活：眼前的事勾起另一件事，一句话写到半途，想到自己刚才说得不对，又拐了一个弯。我们读到的并非一百多条生活建议，而是一个人在纸上想事情的样子。

2016年，四十二岁生日那天，Gay决定用一年时间，试着每天写一篇关于欢喜的短文，后来从中结集成书。日复一日地写，给了这些篇章一种近似闲谈的亲密。读者不必先知道他的完整生平，读着读着，也会熟悉他的花园、朋友和那些容易使他走神的东西。

## 一株番茄苗怎样成为同路人

在一篇短文中，Gay带着朋友送的番茄苗乘飞机。小苗被他一路护着，也引来陌生人的注意；空乘打趣，周围的人露出笑容。临近降落，他伸手保护小苗，忽然想起父亲开车时护住孩子的动作。

如果只把这个故事概括成“人间自有温情”，它就平淡了。真正使人愿意读下去的，是一株植物怎样让这些原本无关的人有了片刻联系。机场里的人各有行程，谁也不需要认识谁。番茄苗却不像一件普通行李：它还活着，需要一点照料，又出现在一个不大适合种菜的地方。人们因此多看了一眼，也有了一句可以说的话。

Gay最后想到父亲，文章便又向前走了一步。这趟旅程不再只是收集陌生人的善意。他正在做一个自己熟悉、却未必事先想过的动作；在这个动作里，旧日的照顾回来了。孩子长大后，父母留下的东西未必总以一句教诲出现，也可能先存在于手臂的反应里。

这也是散文和道理的区别。道理可以预先写好，再找事情来说明；这里却是事情把作者带到了原先没有打算去的地方。若把番茄苗换成任何一种“美好事物”，结论也许仍说得通，但父亲不会以同样的方式出现。具体的东西之所以值得写，正因为它有自己的去路。

这样的文章也不适合读得太赶。Gay的联想有时显得啰嗦，句子刚要结束，又添了半句。不过，如果一心只想找出每篇的中心思想，最有意思的部分恐怕都会被当作枝节删掉。我们认识一个人，也往往靠这些枝节：他对什么格外在意，什么地方会忍不住笑，什么动作忽然令他想家。

## 杂草还是要拔的

最容易误解这本书的地方，是把Gay当成一个能为所有坏事找到好处的人。他在写旋花时，倒先拿这种期待开了自己的玩笑。园丁讨厌这种难缠的杂草，他自己也在拔；他一面设法压住它的蔓延，一面又想写写与它相处的欢喜。

这里有一个很小、却很实在的分寸。他没有因为准备写篇快乐的文章，就宣布杂草其实不妨碍蔬菜生长。花园要照料，草也得继续拔。写作并不负责把现实改判成好事。

这使他的乐观保留了一点粗糙的边缘。我们常在两种说法之间来回：要么承认一件事糟糕，于是觉得关于它没有别的话可说；要么努力寻找好的一面，仿佛这样才算振作。Gay的花园允许两种感受待在一起。他不喜欢杂草带来的麻烦，也没有因此交出整个下午的感受。拔草时想到的词、看到的叶子、忽然冒出的笑意，不必等麻烦彻底解决才发生。

因此，书中那些看似随意的插话有时很重要。作者刚刚作了一个笼统判断，自己的经验便来拆台；他想把事情说得漂亮一点，又发现这样说不够诚实。欢喜不是事先封好的答案，而是在这番往返中逐渐变得具体。

当然，喜欢这种写法，也多少取决于是否愿意和Gay这样的叙述者相处。他热情、爱开玩笑，常常在一条岔路上走得很远。有的读者会被带着走，有的读者则会嫌他始终不肯直奔主题。对一本散文集来说，这种差异并非无关紧要：吸引人的不仅是它谈了什么，也包括你是否愿意把一段时间交给这个声音。

## 一次击掌，并不是所有人的同一种经验

书中有个年轻陌生人看见Gay埋头工作，便和他击掌，为他鼓劲。Gay很喜欢这个举动，但随即交代自己的身体处境：他是个身材高大的非白人男性，怎样的接近会让他感到愉快，与这些条件有关。

这个转折让文章没有停在“陌生人多亲近一点多好”。同一个动作，由谁作出、朝向谁、在什么地方发生，意思可能差得很远。Gay没有为所有人代言；他把自己写进来，反而让读者有位置说：我可能不会这样感觉。

这在他的写作里尤其可贵。讲述快乐，很容易把差异看成扫兴；既然大家正在说美好的事，为何偏要提谁比较安全、谁比较容易被误解？但身体原本就在场。它决定一个人怎样穿过公共空间，也影响别人怎样靠近他。略掉这些，故事才会变得不真实。

Gay的自我修正还改变了作者与读者的关系。他不再是站在前面教我们感受的人，而是一个愿意把感受的来由说清楚的人。读者可以喜欢他的故事，也可以与他不同。这样的亲近，比要求大家对同一件事感动，更有余地。

## 为什么还要一篇一篇地写

接受NPR采访时，Gay说，开始这个计划以前，他以为每天找一件值得欢喜的事会很费力。写了一阵，反而积下了太多材料。这个变化值得留意，却未必需要解释成某种改变人生的方法。更朴素的情况是：因为准备写，他开始留意原先会匆匆放过的事；而留意之后，又多了可以写的东西。

不过，留意并不自动等于文章。在另一次访谈中，他谈到给每天的初稿留出很短的时间，也谈到朋友对自己写作的帮助。成书后那种仿佛顺口说来的语气，背后仍有写作者的取舍。日常经验不会自己排好队走上纸面，要找到从一件事通往另一件事的路，才能让别人也跟着看见。

所以，这本书不只有题材上的亲切，还有写法上的示范。它让人发现，所谓微不足道，有时只是我们尚未找到讲述它的办法。一株苗、一场不好意思夸耀的球赛，都可能打开记忆，也可能暴露自己的虚荣。等这些东西被写出来，生活就不再只有重大成就和重大挫折值得记账。

Gay并未因为专注这些小事，就不知道更大的世界正在发生什么。他这一年的写作跨过了2016年美国大选。在采访中，他承认公共事件会使自己消沉；继续写欢喜，是他有意保持的一份注意。这个选择有它的范围，不能承担对时局的全部回答。但一个人每天实际遇见的照顾、偶然和笑声，也不该因为无法代表全局，就从他的经验里被取消。

《欢喜之书》适合慢慢翻，未必需要按顺序一口气读完。读它最好的理由，恐怕也不是学会比从前更乐观，而是认识一位会把事情越看越细的作者。跟着他看了一阵，再回头想起那场二十一比零的篮球赛，仍然会想笑。笑过之后，才发现他已经把自己也放进了故事：那个想显得厉害、又知道自己实在没有那么厉害的人。
en_body:
Ross Gay and a friend win a basketball game twenty-one to zero. He recounts the victory with considerable pleasure, then supplies a detail: their opponents were twelve-year-olds. A girl watching is unimpressed.

The embarrassment gives us a good introduction to The Book of Delights. Gay does not make delight especially noble, or hurry to extract a lesson from basketball. He enjoys his moment, then lets us see how ridiculous that enjoyment is. On the page he is frequently overenthusiastic, full of associations, running after something he has just said to correct it. What pleases him can seem inconsequential. His gift is making us want to hear exactly how inconsequential it was.

This is not quite what the title might lead us to expect. A book of delights sounds like a guide to finding happiness in ordinary things. Gay certainly writes about plants, food, and strangers’ kindness, but he is first a poet. Much of the pleasure lies in watching him bring something alive in language. One event recalls another; halfway through a sentence he realizes that the first version was not quite right and turns aside. These are not a hundred or so pieces of advice. They show a person thinking on paper.

On his forty-second birthday in 2016, Gay decided to spend a year trying to write a short essay about delight each day. A selection became this book. The continuing practice lends the pieces the intimacy of conversation. Without first studying his biography, we gradually come to know his garden, his friends, and the things that distract him.

## How a tomato plant becomes a fellow traveler

In one essay Gay takes a tomato seedling, a gift from a friend, onto an airplane. He protects it along the way, attracting strangers’ attention, an attendant’s joke, and smiles. As landing approaches, he puts out an arm to shield it and remembers his father doing something similar for a child in a car.

Summarize this as evidence of human warmth and much of its interest disappears. What holds us is the way a plant briefly connects people with otherwise separate concerns. Everyone in an airport has somewhere to go. Nobody needs to know anybody else. The seedling, however, is not quite ordinary luggage. It is alive, requires care, and has turned up somewhere distinctly unsuitable for growing vegetables. It gives people something to notice and something to say.

The memory of his father carries the essay further. This is no longer merely an inventory of kindness from strangers. Gay finds himself performing a familiar movement without necessarily having thought about it first. An old experience of being protected returns through the act of protecting. What parents leave behind need not arrive as a remembered instruction. It can survive in an arm’s response.

Here we can see a difference between an essay and a lesson. A lesson may be settled in advance, awaiting an illustration. Here the event takes the writer somewhere he had not planned to go. Replace the seedling with any “beautiful thing” and the general conclusion might survive, but the father would not appear in quite the same way. A particular thing is worth writing about because it has its own directions.

Such essays also reward an unhurried reading. Gay’s associations can feel excessive: a sentence almost ends, then acquires another clause. But a reader searching only for the main point may discard the best parts as digressions. Often we come to know someone through just such details—what matters disproportionately to him, what makes him laugh, what suddenly reminds him of home.

## The weeds still have to come out

It is easy to mistake Gay for someone who can find a benefit in every bad thing. His writing about bindweed plays with that expectation. Gardeners dislike this persistent weed, and he is pulling it up too. Even as he tries to control its spread, he wants to write about delight in his encounter with it.

The distinction is small but practical. Preparing a cheerful essay does not lead him to declare that the weed poses no problem for his vegetables. The garden still needs tending. The weed still needs pulling. Writing does not have to reclassify reality as good news.

His optimism consequently keeps some rough edges. We often alternate between acknowledging that something is bad, as though nothing else could be said about it, and searching for its bright side, as though that were the only way to recover. Gay’s garden accommodates more than one feeling. He dislikes the trouble the weed causes without surrendering the whole afternoon to that dislike. The words that occur to him, the leaves he notices, the sudden amusement need not wait until the problem is solved.

This makes apparently casual interruptions important. A broad statement has barely appeared before experience challenges it. He wants to put something attractively, then discovers that the attractive version is not quite honest. Delight becomes specific through this movement back and forth, rather than arriving as a sealed answer.

Enjoying the book will partly depend on enjoying this narrator’s company. He is warm, humorous, and inclined to travel a long way down a side road. Some readers will follow gladly; others will wish he would get to the point. In an essay collection this is not incidental. What draws us is both the subject and our willingness to spend time with a particular voice.

## A high five is not the same experience for everyone

A young stranger sees Gay absorbed in work and offers him an encouraging high five. Gay welcomes the gesture, then specifies his own situation: he is a large nonwhite man. What kinds of approach feel pleasant to him have something to do with those circumstances.

The turn prevents the piece from ending at “Wouldn’t it be nice if strangers were friendlier?” Who makes a gesture, toward whom, and where can change its meaning substantially. Gay does not speak for everyone. By putting himself more fully into the account, he leaves readers room to say that they might feel differently.

This is particularly valuable in writing about pleasure. Differences can easily be treated as spoiling the mood. If we are discussing lovely things, why bring up who feels safer or who is more likely to be misunderstood? Yet bodies were present all along. They shape how someone moves through public space and how others approach. Omitting them would make the story less truthful.

Gay’s correction also changes his relationship with readers. He becomes less a teacher of appropriate feeling than someone willing to explain where his feeling comes from. We can enjoy his story without sharing his response. This allows a less coercive intimacy than asking everyone to be moved by the same thing.

## Why keep writing, one piece at a time?

In an NPR interview Gay said that before beginning he expected it to be difficult to find something delightful every day. After a while, he had too much material. The change is worth noticing without turning it into a life-changing formula. More simply, preparing to write made him attend to things he might otherwise have passed over. Paying attention, in turn, gave him more to write about.

Attention does not automatically produce an essay. In another interview he discussed both the short time allowed for daily first drafts and the help of friends in his writing. The apparently conversational voice still involves choices. Experience does not arrange itself on a page. A writer must find a path from one thing to another that someone else can follow.

The book therefore offers something beyond approachable subjects. Apparently insignificant experiences may be ones we have not yet found a way to tell. A seedling or a basketball victory not worth boasting about can open a memory or expose vanity. Once written, they expand a record of life otherwise dominated by major achievements and setbacks.

Gay’s attention to small things does not imply ignorance of larger events. His writing year crossed the 2016 American election. In interview he acknowledged being discouraged by public events; continuing to write about delight was a deliberate commitment of attention. That choice has limits and cannot answer every political question. Yet the care, accidents, and laughter a person actually encounters need not disappear from his experience simply because they do not represent the whole world.

This is a book to dip into, not necessarily finish in order at once. Its best invitation may be to meet a writer who looks more closely, rather than to become more optimistic. After following him awhile, the twenty-one-to-zero game is still funny. And then we notice that he has included himself in the joke: the person who would like to seem impressive, and knows he is not quite as impressive as he would like.
